q: The consistent theme about clustering algorithms, per L8:
a: When data is easily clusterable, most algorithms work well; when it isn't, no algorithm finds good clusters
w: k-means always finds the best clusters
e: That's why the course doesn't spend more time on clustering.

q: In hard clustering, the two goals are:
a: Small 'width' (points within a cluster are close) and large 'split' (points in different clusters are far)
w: Equal cluster sizes and few clusters
e: Overall we want split/width (or split − width) to be large.

q: Which hard-clustering condition is relaxed in SOFT clustering?
a: Clusters must be disjoint (Sᵢ ∩ Sⱼ = ∅)
w: Every cluster is a subset of X
The clusters' union is all of X
e: In soft clustering, a point can partially belong to several clusters (e.g., EM).

q: The basic hierarchical agglomerative clustering loop is:
a: Start with every point as its own cluster; repeatedly merge the two closest clusters while they're 'close enough'
w: Start with one cluster and split it
Pick k random centers and reassign
e: You must define both 'closest' (an inter-cluster distance) and 'close enough' (a stopping rule).

q: Which is NOT a listed option for the distance between clusters?
a: Number of points in the larger cluster
w: Distance between closest pair of points
Distance between furthest pair of points
Average distance over all cross-cluster pairs
e: Others: distance between centers (mean, centerpoint, MEB center), radius of the merged MEB, etc. Ties can drastically change results.

q: Stopping when the merged cluster's density increases too much compared to the single clusters is a variant of the:
a: 'Elbow' technique
e: Other stopping rules: an absolute threshold τ, diameter/radius thresholds, density thresholds, or reaching k clusters.

q: What's the advantage of recording the full merge hierarchy?
a: You don't need to choose when to stop up front; you can 'chop off the top of the tree' later
e: The most famous example is phylogenetic trees.

q: Naive centroid-based HAC on n points takes O(n³). With a priority queue it takes:
a: O(n² log n)
e: Centroids update in O(1) by storing count and center, then merging via weighted average. Still slow compared to other methods.

q: In DBScan, a point x is a core point if:
a: At least τ (minPts) points are within radius r (ε) of x
w: It's the mean of its cluster
e: All core points end up in clusters.

q: In DBScan's graph, there's an edge between xᵢ and xⱼ when they're within distance r AND:
a: At least one of them is a core point
e: Clusters are connected components. Two nearby non-core points aren't connected, and isolated points belong to no cluster.

q: A main advantage of DBScan is that clusters:
a: Adapt to the shape of the data, connecting via paths through dense regions
e: Downsides: no automatic way to pick r and τ, and it assumes density is consistent across the dataset.

q: DBScan is usually efficient because:
a: Core-point checks and neighbor finding use fast NN search (e.g., LSH), and it skips building an explicit hierarchy
w: It always runs in O(log n)
e: Worst case is still quadratic in n.

q: Is k-means an algorithm?
a: No, it's a problem formulation (Lloyd's algorithm is the usual way to attack it)
e: k-means minimizes Σ d(φ_C(x), x)².

q: Match the objective: minimize the MAXIMUM assignment distance.
a: k-center
e: k-means minimizes the sum of squared distances, and k-median the sum of distances. k-medoid is like k-median with centers restricted to data points.

q: Which formulation is most robust to outliers but has no simple iterative algorithm like Lloyd's or Gonzalez?
a: k-median
e: Its recentering step is the Fermat-Weber problem, which is surprisingly complicated (approximate it with gradient descent).

q: Gonzalez's greedy algorithm for k-center picks each new center as:
a: The point furthest from its currently assigned center
w: The point closest to all others
e: 'Be greedy, and avoid your neighbors!'

q: Gonzalez's algorithm gives what guarantee for k-center, and in what time?
a: A 2-approximation in O(kn) time, for any metric
w: Exact optimum in O(n log n)
e: Finding better than a factor 2 is NP-hard in general metrics. Downside: centers biased to the 'edges' of the data.

q: Lloyd's algorithm alternates which two steps?
a: Assign each point to its nearest center; then move each center to the average of its assigned points
w: Split the largest cluster; merge the smallest
Pick the furthest point; add it as a center
e: It repeats until the centers stop changing. That takes roughly Rnk steps for R rounds.

q: Why must Lloyd's algorithm terminate?
a: Cost strictly decreases, and there are finitely many (≈ nᵏ) possible clusterings
e: Worst-case it could be exponential, but usually R ≈ 10 is fine.

q: Does Lloyd's algorithm 'solve' the k-means problem?
a: No: it can get stuck in a local optimum, so it's typically re-run with random initializations
w: No, it doesn't decrease the cost
e: Keep the lowest-cost result over several runs.

q: Why is initializing Lloyd's with a random partition's averages a poor choice?
a: It biases all initial centers toward the center of the whole dataset (Central Limit Theorem)
e: Random k points need about k log k (coupon collectors) to hit each cluster. Gonzalez biases toward outliers.

q: k-means++ chooses each next center with probability proportional to:
a: d(x, nearest existing center)²
e: It's like Gonzalez but not fully greedy. It gives an O(log n) approximation and is the default in most libraries.

q: Why does Lloyd's recentering step only work with squared Euclidean distance?
a: The average is the argmin of Σ‖c − x‖² only for squared Euclidean distance
e: For other distances, restrict C ⊂ X (k-medoid) or solve harder center problems.

q: All else being equal, k-means tends to produce clusters that are:
a: Roughly equal-sized (based on distance to centers, not density)
e: It's also more affected by outliers than k-median.

q: A Gaussian mixture model with every covariance Σᵢ = I is equivalent to:
a: The k-means problem
e: In general each cluster is G(µᵢ, Σᵢ), with Σᵢ the sum of outer products (x − µᵢ)(x − µᵢ)ᵀ.

q: In EM for Gaussian mixtures, each point gets weight wᵢ(x) = ?
a: fᵢ(x) / Σⱼ fⱼ(x): a soft (partial) assignment
e: Means and covariances are then re-estimated with weighted averages.

q: Expectation-Maximization is useful when:
a: The true objective is messy/non-convex but splits into alternating steps that each have (near) closed forms
w: The problem has a single closed-form solution
e: EM alternates partial assignment with model (mean and covariance) estimation.
